founded.what: The year Pol Roger, a young man of seventeen or eighteen, made his first sale of wine, in January, by the house's own account.

place: Épernay, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it grows part of its fruit, buys the rest from growers in some thirty crus and makes the wine itself in its Épernay cellars.

story: Pol Roger made his first sale of wine in January 1849, by the house's account, and in 1851 moved the business from Aÿ to Épernay. When he died of pneumonia in 1899 his two sons took over, and on 23 February 1900 part of the cellars collapsed, taking down hundreds of casks and outbuildings with them. That year the sons were allowed to take the surname Pol-Roger in honour of their father. After the liberation of Paris, a member of the family was introduced to Sir Winston Churchill (1874 to 1965) at the British Embassy, where the house's 1928 was served, and a friendship followed that lasted until his death. On Churchill's death in 1965, on the family's instructions, every Pol Roger label bound for Britain was bordered in black. The house made the first vintage of Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill in 1975, the tenth anniversary of his death, and launched it in 1984 at Blenheim Palace, his birthplace, in magnum alone and for Britain alone; standard bottles and other markets followed from the 1979 vintage. The 2015, by the house, is the twenty first vintage of the cuvée.

style.line: Poised and fine rather than powerful: musts settled twice, slow cool fermentations in steel, and long ageing in deep, cold chalk cellars beneath Épernay keep the wines tight and the mousse fine.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay in about equal parts for Brut Réserve, from some thirty crus, by the house; Grand Cru Pinot Noir and Chardonnay alone for Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill.
style.reserve: About a quarter reserve wines in Brut Réserve, by the house, from at least three vintages among some thirty base wines.
style.vessels: Stainless steel: a slow, cool fermentation below 18 degrees, each variety and each village kept apart until the blend, by the house.
style.malolactic: A full malolactic conversion before the final blend, by the house's sheets.
style.lees: At least four years on the lees for Brut Réserve, by the house, in cellars 33 metres below the street, every bottle riddled by hand.
style.dosage: 8 grams a litre for Brut Réserve and 7 for Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill 2015, by the house.

nv.name: Brut Réserve
nv.note: The non vintage Brut, known in Britain as White Foil: Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay in about equal thirds, with about a quarter reserve wines, by the house.

cuvee.name: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill

first.what: The first vintage, made for the tenth anniversary of Churchill's death and launched in 1984 at Blenheim Palace, in magnum alone.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in vintages the house judges worthy and released later than its other vintage wines: the 2015 is the twenty first vintage since 1975, by the house, and merchants list a 2018 after it.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Grand Cru vineyards, Pinot Noir leading, by the house; the proportions have never been published.
cuvee.sites: Grand Cru vineyards of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, by the house, which has never named the villages or the parcels.
cuvee.making: The musts are settled twice, the second time cold in steel at 6 degrees over a day, then fermented slowly below 18 degrees in stainless steel, each village apart, with a full malolactic conversion before blending. The second fermentation runs at about 9 degrees in the deepest cellars, 33 metres down, and the bottles are riddled by hand. The 2015 was dosed at 7 grams a litre.
cuvee.lees: At least eight years by Decanter and The World of Fine Wine; about a decade in the house's own words.
cuvee.young: Ripe pear, white peach and candied tangerine peel over apple pastry and hazelnut, with a firm Pinot Noir frame and a long, chalky close.
cuvee.aged: The older vintages turn to hay, quince and yellow fruits, then to cèpes, caramel and truffle, in The World of Fine Wine's verticals; bottles of the early vintages vary.

forms.name: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill Édition Vinothèque
forms.note: The same vintage wine held far longer in the house's cellars before release, such as the 2002 and the 2004.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Pol Roger is the family house of Épernay, dating from a first sale of wine in 1849. Its cellars run deep and cold beneath the town, and every bottle there is turned by hand. The story guests love is Sir Winston Churchill, a friend of the family and a loyal drinker of the house's Champagne. When he died in 1965, the house's labels for Britain were bordered in black. The style is poised and fine rather than heavy. Brut Réserve, called White Foil in Britain, is the bottle most guests know, and Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is the prestige cuvée.
table.house10: Pol Roger is the Épernay house of 1849 with deep, cold cellars, the Champagne Sir Winston Churchill drank and the cuvée named for him.
table.cuvee45: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is the prestige Champagne of Pol Roger, made in tribute to a friend of the family. Its first vintage was 1975, ten years after his death, and it was launched in 1984 at Blenheim Palace. It is Grand Cru Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Pinot Noir leading. The house has never published the blend, and it is released later than its other vintage wines. Expect ripe pear, candied tangerine peel and apple pastry, with a long, chalky finish. I serve it cool rather than ice cold, in a white wine glass.
table.sale: If you want a Champagne with a story for the table, Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is Pol Roger's tribute to its most loyal friend, Pinot Noir led and long aged. May I bring a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is Pol Roger's Pinot Noir led vintage tribute to Churchill, first made in 1975.
table.cuvee20: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is Pol Roger's prestige vintage, Grand Cru Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, its blend never published. It is released later than the house's other vintages, with ripe pear, candied tangerine peel and a long, chalky close.

guests.q: Did Churchill really drink Pol Roger?
guests.a: Yes, by the house's account and Churchill's own society: he met the family at the British Embassy in Paris after the liberation, a friendship followed, and the house bordered its British labels in black when he died in 1965.
Grand Cru Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir leading. The house has never published the proportions or the villages, so any figure you read elsewhere is a guess.

guests.q: When was the first one made?
guests.a: The 1975 vintage, for the tenth anniversary of his death. It was launched in 1984 at Blenheim Palace, where he was born, in magnum only.
No, it is a Brut: the house gave the 2015 7 grams of sugar a litre, which reads as dry at the table.

traps: Sir Winston Churchill is always vintage dated, not a non-vintage prestige blend.
It is Pinot Noir dominant, not a blanc de blancs.
The blend has never been published, so any percentage quoted is invention.
Sir Winston Churchill is Pol Roger's, of Épernay; Dom Pérignon, the other prestige cuvée named for a man, is Moët & Chandon's.

sheet.label: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill
sheet.note: The sheet and the label agree on the name; the label adds the word Cuvée before it. The wine is always a vintage, so the label also carries its year.

questions.q: A guest asks for the prestige cuvée named for the wartime prime minister who was a friend of the house that made it. Which house pours it?
questions.exp: Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill is Pol Roger's tribute, first made in 1975. Louis Roederer's Cristal was made for a Tsar, Moët & Chandon's Dom Pérignon is named for a monk and Veuve Clicquot's La Grande Dame for a widow.

questions.q: Why were Pol Roger's labels for Britain bordered in black from 1965?
opts: In mourning for Sir Winston Churchill
For the end of the Second World War
questions.exp: Churchill died in 1965 and the family bordered the British labels in black in his memory. The founder died in 1899, the cellars collapsed in February 1900 and the war ended twenty years before.

questions.q: What has Pol Roger said of the blend of Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill?
opts: Grand Cru Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Pinot Noir leading
Equal thirds of the three grapes
Chardonnay alone from the Côte des Blancs
Mostly Meunier from the Vallée de la Marne
questions.exp: The house names Grand Cru Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with Pinot Noir leading, and has never published the proportions. Equal thirds is Brut Réserve, the house's non vintage, and a Chardonnay alone wine would be a Blanc de Blancs.

report: Built on the library's p-pol-roger and w-sir-winston-churchill, contradicting neither; their three traps on the cuvée are kept word for word, and no proportion of the blend is given, by the library's own trap.
Pol Roger himself is named only as the label: his birth year was not found, the house giving his age in 1849 as seventeen on one page and eighteen on another; the sons' names are left out.

The family member Churchill met is described, not named: her dates were not found in two sources (one obituary dates her death to 2000). The year of the meeting is 1944 by most accounts and 12 November 1945 by one citing a diary, so the record says after the liberation of Paris.

The cellar collapse: the house's press release dates it 23 February 1900; the losses are given as 500 casks by one page and up to a million and a half bottles by another, so the record says hundreds of casks.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; they are inferred from the house buying from some thirty crus, and a refuter should read one.
Lees: Decanter and The World of Fine Wine give at least eight years; the house's page speaks of a decade, which may describe the Vinothèque edition, so both are given.
The rhythm: the house calls the 2015 the twenty first vintage; merchants list a 2018, one calling it the twenty second and another the twenty first, so the record names the 2018 without a count.
Brut Réserve's rest after disgorging, three months by the main site and nine by the British site, is left out.
The young glass draws on merchants' notes on the 2018 and the library's glass (apple pastry, hazelnut, a chalky close); the aged glass on The World of Fine Wine's verticals.
cuvee.bottle is empty: the black border was on the house's British labels after 1965, not a bottle of the cuvée, and it is told in the story.
Every style field is stated, from the house's sheets for Brut Réserve and the cuvée.
